title: Investigating causality between principal components in protein dynamics
authors: Debarshi Banerjee, Ali Hassanali, Alessandro Laio
abstract: Principal component analysis (PCA) is widely used to characterize collective protein motions from molecular dynamics (MD) simulations. While PCA identifies the dominant modes of structural fluctuation, it does not reveal whether different principal components (PCs) causally influence each other. Here, we investigate this question using a recently introduced causal-discovery framework [Del Tatto et al, PNAS 2024], which allows to infer putative causal asymmetries between high-dimensional time series. We apply this approach to long-timescale MD trajectories of two proteins. By analyzing relationships among PCs, we construct directed networks describing how PCs influence one another across time scales. These directional relationships, whose existence is a necessary condition for the presence of a causal link, are not captured by conventional covariance-based analyses and provide information that is complementary to PCA and Time-lagged Independent Component Analysis (TICA). Our results suggest that our causal inference approach can uncover previously hidden aspects of the dynamical organization of protein motions and offer a new perspective on this very popular class of collective variables.
summary: This work applies advanced causal inference techniques to molecular dynamics simulations of protein folding. By quantifying directional information flow between Principal Components, the authors demonstrate that collective motions exhibit a directed causal structure, suggesting that slow structural fluctuations dictate subsequent faster movements within the protein's conformational landscape.
main_problem: The study investigates whether different Principal Components (PCs) derived from protein dynamics simulations causally influence each other over time, moving beyond simple correlation measures.
main_result: The causal inference approach reveals directed information flow ($	ext{PC1} 	o \{	ext{PC2}, 	ext{PC3}\}$) in both ubiquitin and NTL9, suggesting that the slowest collective mode drives subsequent faster fluctuations. This directional structure is not captured by conventional covariance-based analyses.
method: The core method employs a causal-discovery framework based on Information Imbalance (IG), which quantifies predictive asymmetry between time series derived from MD simulations.
model_or_system: The system studied is the dynamics of proteins, specifically ubiquitin and NTL9, simulated using Molecular Dynamics (MD) trajectories. The analysis reduces the high-dimensional conformational space into a set of collective variables represented by Principal Components (PCs).
key_observables: Pairwise Integrated Information Transfer (IGT), Brüschweiler collectivity index ($\kappa_k$), and time-lagged covariance matrices $\Gamma(	au)$.
important_parameters: Time lags ($	au$) up to the microsecond scale, and the magnitude of the Imbalance Gain ($	ext{IG}$).
main_assumptions: The inferred causal links are putative; they suggest necessary but not sufficient conditions for true causality due to potential unobserved confounders.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate autocorrelation functions showing decorrelation timescales, pairwise IG curves demonstrating directional asymmetry (e.g., $	ext{PC1} 	o 	ext{PC2}$), and resulting causal graphs mapping the strongest information flow paths.
paper_structure: The paper introduces PCA/TICA limitations, details the application of the Information Imbalance framework to calculate directed couplings between PCs for two proteins (Ubiquitin and NTL9), presents results showing directional influence from slow modes to fast modes, and concludes by discussing implications for understanding protein dynamics organization.
why_interesting: While focused on biomolecules, the methodology—using information-theoretic measures like IG to infer directed relationships in high-dimensional time series—is a powerful tool applicable to analyzing complex non-equilibrium dynamics in many-body systems beyond proteins.
